The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For a supervised prediction problem with joint law $P$, the **population risk** of any measurable predictor $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ (in particular, every $f\in\mathcal F$) is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_P(f):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(f(x),y)\,P(d(x,y))\in[0,+\infty].$$
For an ordered sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_m,y_m))$ of length $m\ge1$, the **empirical risk** or **training risk** of any such $f$ is
$$\widehat R_S(f):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\ell(f(x_i),y_i)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Neither definition assumes finite risk. The sum uses extended nonnegative arithmetic; since $m\ge1$, any summand equal to $+\infty$ makes the empirical risk $+\infty$.

Let $\mathcal Z$ be an observation set, let $\mathcal H$ be a set of hypotheses, and let $L:\mathcal H\times\mathcal Z\to[0,\infty)$ be a loss. A deterministic size-indexed learning rule consists, for every integer $n\ge1$ and every retained index set $J\subseteq[n]$, of a map $A_{n,J}$ from the indexed observations $(z_j)_{j\in J}$ to $\mathcal H$; the original sample size $n$ remains an input to this rule. For $S=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$ write $A_S:=A_{n,[n]}(S)$ and $A_{S\setminus i}:=A_{n,[n]\setminus\{i\}}(S|_{[n]\setminus\{i\}})$ for the output after deleting indexed observation $i$. The rule is permutation-invariant if simultaneous reordering of the observations and relabeling of their retained indices leaves each output unchanged. Given a nonnegative sequence $(\beta_n)_{n\ge1}$, the rule has uniform deletion stability with coefficients $(\beta_n)$ if, for every $n\ge1$, every $S\in\mathcal Z^n$, every $i\in[n]$, and every $z\in\mathcal Z$,

$$
|L(A_S,z)-L(A_{S\setminus i},z)|\le\beta_n.
$$

The sequence is nonincreasing when $\beta_{n+1}\le\beta_n$ for every $n\ge1$. This is the deletion convention. If $S'$ differs from $S$ only at coordinate $i$, then $S\setminus i=S'\setminus i$, and the triangle inequality gives $|L(A_S,z)-L(A_{S'},z)|\le2\beta_n$ for every $z$; the resulting replacement bound has coefficient $2\beta_n$.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ and $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ be measurable instance and label spaces, let $P$ be a probability measure on $\mathsf Z=\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a class of measurable predictors with measurable loss $\ell:\mathbb R\times\mathsf Y\to[0,\infty)$. For $f\in\mathcal F$ and $z=(x,y)$ write $L_f(z)=\ell(f(x),y)$, $R_P(f)=\int_{\mathsf Z}L_f(z)\,P(dz)$, and $\widehat R_S(f)=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^mL_f(Z_i)$. Let $S=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ have product law $P^m$, with $m\ge1$, and let $A$ be a deterministic, permutation-invariant size-indexed learning rule that outputs members of $\mathcal F$ and whose sample-dependent loss and risk maps are measurable. Assume $0\le L_{A_T}(z)\le M<\infty$ for every full or deleted sample $T$ and every $z\in\mathsf Z$, and assume $A$ has uniform deletion stability with a finite nonincreasing sequence $(\beta_n)_{n\ge1}$. Define $R_{\mathrm{loo}}(A,S)=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m L_{A_{S\setminus i}}(Z_i)$, using the size-$m$ deletion output. Then

$$\mathbb E_{S\sim P^m}\bigl[R_P(A_S)-\widehat R_S(A_S)\bigr]\le2\beta_m\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbb E_{S\sim P^m}\bigl[R_P(A_S)-R_{\mathrm{loo}}(A,S)\bigr]\le\beta_m.$$

Moreover, for every sample $S$ and index $i\in[m]$,

$$|R_P(A_S)-R_P(A_{S\setminus i})|\le\beta_m.$$

All three conclusions are choice-free.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Assume AC. Let $n\ge1$, let $Z_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be independent random elements, meaning measurable maps ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]), with laws $\mu_i$ given by pushforward ([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]). Put $\mu=\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mu_i$ on the finite product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). Let $f:\prod_{i=1}^nS_i\to\mathbb R$ be product-measurable with $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$. Suppose finite deterministic constants $c_i\ge0$ satisfy
$$|f(z_1,\ldots,z_i,\ldots,z_n)-f(z_1,\ldots,z_i',\ldots,z_n)|\le c_i$$
for every fixed setting of the other coordinates and every $z_i,z_i'$. The independent product-law theorem identifies the law of $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$ as $\mu$. Applying change of variables for expectation first to $|f|$ and then to $f$ makes $f(Z)$ integrable and gives $\mathbb E f(Z)=\int f\,d\mu$. Put $V=\sum_{i=1}^n c_i^2$. For $t>0$, if $V>0$ then
$$\mathbb P\bigl(f(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)-\mathbb E f(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)\ge t\bigr)\le\exp\!\left(-\frac{2t^2}{V}\right),$$
and if $V=0$ this probability is $0$. The same bound holds for the lower tail, so the two-sided probability is at most $2e^{-2t^2/V}$ when $V>0$.

derivations.claim: Fix an index $k$ and let $S'$ be any sample that differs from $S$ only at coordinate $k$. Their retained samples $S\setminus k$ and $S'\setminus k$ coincide. By [F4], $|R_P(A_S)-R_P(A_{S'})|\le|R_P(A_S)-R_P(A_{S\setminus k})|+|R_P(A_{S'\setminus k})-R_P(A_{S'})|\le2\beta_m$. For every $j\ne k$, the two loss terms at the common test point $Z_j$ differ by at most $2\beta_m$, by [F2] through the same deleted output. The two $k$th loss terms each lie in $[0,M]$, so their difference is at most $M$. Hence $|\widehat R_S(A_S)-\widehat R_{S'}(A_{S'})|\le 2(m-1)\beta_m/m+M/m\le2\beta_m+M/m$. For $\Phi(S)=R_P(A_S)-\widehat R_S(A_S)$ this yields the coordinate oscillation $|\Phi(S)-\Phi(S')|\le4\beta_m+M/m$.

Fix an index $k$ and samples $S,S'$ differing only at coordinate $k$. The risk term in $\Psi(S)=R_P(A_S)-R_{\mathrm{loo}}(A,S)$ changes by at most $2\beta_m$ by [F4]. In the leave-one-out average, the $k$th term uses the same deleted training sample for $S$ and $S'$, and its test losses differ by at most $M$. For $j\ne k$, the two deleted training samples $S\setminus j$ and $S'\setminus j$ have the same $m-2$ common observations and the two alternative $k$th observations. Form a size-$m$ indexed sample $T$ from those $m-2$ common observations and both alternatives. Up to permutation, each of the two deleted training samples is obtained by deleting one of the alternatives from $T$. Permutation invariance and [F2] therefore bound their loss change at the common test point $Z_j$ by $2\beta_m$. When $m=1$ there are no indices $j\ne k$, so only the $k$th term occurs. Thus the leave-one-out average changes by at most $2(m-1)\beta_m/m+M/m\le2\beta_m+M/m$, and $|\Psi(S)-\Psi(S')|\le4\beta_m+M/m$.

Put $c=4\beta_m+M/m$. If $c=0$, then $M=\beta_m=0$ and every loss and both gaps vanish. If $c>0$, then $\Phi$ is bounded, measurable, and integrable by [A2]. Since $0<\delta<1$, [F5]–[F6] give $\log(1/\delta)>0$, so $t=c\sqrt{m\log(1/\delta)/2}>0$. The product law $P^m$ makes the coordinates independent by [F3], and [F7] with all $m$ coordinate bounds equal to $c$ gives $\mathbb P\{\Phi-\mathbb E\Phi\ge t\}\le\exp(-2t^2/(mc^2))=\delta$. By [F4], outside this event $\Phi\le2\beta_m+t=2\beta_m+(4m\beta_m+M)\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/(2m)}$. Together with the $c=0$ case this proves the first probability bound.

With $c=4\beta_m+M/m$, the case $c=0$ again has zero losses and zero gaps. If $c>0$, [A2] makes $\Psi$ bounded, measurable, and integrable. Since $0<\delta<1$, [F5]–[F6] give $\log(1/\delta)>0$. The product law $P^m$ makes the coordinates independent by [F3], and [F7] with coordinate bounds $c$ gives $\mathbb P\{\Psi-\mathbb E\Psi\ge c\sqrt{m\log(1/\delta)/2}\}\le\delta$. By [F4], $\mathbb E\Psi\le\beta_m$, so outside this event $\Psi\le\beta_m+(4m\beta_m+M)\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/(2m)}$. This proves the second probability bound, separately from the first.

itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For a supervised prediction problem with joint law $P$, the **population risk** of any measurable predictor $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ (in particular, every $f\in\mathcal F$) is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_P(f):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(f(x),y)\,P(d(x,y))\in[0,+\infty].$$
For an ordered sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_m,y_m))$ of length $m\ge1$, the **empirical risk** or **training risk** of any such $f$ is
$$\widehat R_S(f):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\ell(f(x_i),y_i)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Neither definition assumes finite risk. The sum uses extended nonnegative arithmetic; since $m\ge1$, any summand equal to $+\infty$ makes the empirical risk $+\infty$.

Let $\mathcal Z$ be an observation set, let $\mathcal H$ be a set of hypotheses, and let $L:\mathcal H\times\mathcal Z\to[0,\infty)$ be a loss. A deterministic size-indexed learning rule consists, for every integer $n\ge1$ and every retained index set $J\subseteq[n]$, of a map $A_{n,J}$ from the indexed observations $(z_j)_{j\in J}$ to $\mathcal H$; the original sample size $n$ remains an input to this rule. For $S=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$ write $A_S:=A_{n,[n]}(S)$ and $A_{S\setminus i}:=A_{n,[n]\setminus\{i\}}(S|_{[n]\setminus\{i\}})$ for the output after deleting indexed observation $i$. The rule is permutation-invariant if simultaneous reordering of the observations and relabeling of their retained indices leaves each output unchanged. Given a nonnegative sequence $(\beta_n)_{n\ge1}$, the rule has uniform deletion stability with coefficients $(\beta_n)$ if, for every $n\ge1$, every $S\in\mathcal Z^n$, every $i\in[n]$, and every $z\in\mathcal Z$,

$$
|L(A_S,z)-L(A_{S\setminus i},z)|\le\beta_n.
$$

The sequence is nonincreasing when $\beta_{n+1}\le\beta_n$ for every $n\ge1$. This is the deletion convention. If $S'$ differs from $S$ only at coordinate $i$, then $S\setminus i=S'\setminus i$, and the triangle inequality gives $|L(A_S,z)-L(A_{S'},z)|\le2\beta_n$ for every $z$; the resulting replacement bound has coefficient $2\beta_n$.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ and $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ be measurable instance and label spaces, let $P$ be a probability measure on $\mathsf Z=\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a class of measurable predictors with measurable loss $\ell:\mathbb R\times\mathsf Y\to[0,\infty)$. For $f\in\mathcal F$ and $z=(x,y)$ write $L_f(z)=\ell(f(x),y)$, $R_P(f)=\int_{\mathsf Z}L_f(z)\,P(dz)$, and $\widehat R_S(f)=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^mL_f(Z_i)$. Let $S=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ have product law $P^m$, with $m\ge1$, and let $A$ be a deterministic, permutation-invariant size-indexed learning rule that outputs members of $\mathcal F$ and whose sample-dependent loss and risk maps are measurable. Assume $0\le L_{A_T}(z)\le M<\infty$ for every full or deleted sample $T$ and every $z\in\mathsf Z$, and assume $A$ has uniform deletion stability with a finite nonincreasing sequence $(\beta_n)_{n\ge1}$. Define $R_{\mathrm{loo}}(A,S)=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m L_{A_{S\setminus i}}(Z_i)$, using the size-$m$ deletion output. Then

$$\mathbb E_{S\sim P^m}\bigl[R_P(A_S)-\widehat R_S(A_S)\bigr]\le2\beta_m\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbb E_{S\sim P^m}\bigl[R_P(A_S)-R_{\mathrm{loo}}(A,S)\bigr]\le\beta_m.$$

Moreover, for every sample $S$ and index $i\in[m]$,

$$|R_P(A_S)-R_P(A_{S\setminus i})|\le\beta_m.$$

All three conclusions are choice-free.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Assume AC. Let $n\ge1$, let $Z_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be independent random elements, meaning measurable maps ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]), with laws $\mu_i$ given by pushforward ([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]). Put $\mu=\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mu_i$ on the finite product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). Let $f:\prod_{i=1}^nS_i\to\mathbb R$ be product-measurable with $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$. Suppose finite deterministic constants $c_i\ge0$ satisfy
$$|f(z_1,\ldots,z_i,\ldots,z_n)-f(z_1,\ldots,z_i',\ldots,z_n)|\le c_i$$
for every fixed setting of the other coordinates and every $z_i,z_i'$. The independent product-law theorem identifies the law of $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$ as $\mu$. Applying change of variables for expectation first to $|f|$ and then to $f$ makes $f(Z)$ integrable and gives $\mathbb E f(Z)=\int f\,d\mu$. Put $V=\sum_{i=1}^n c_i^2$. For $t>0$, if $V>0$ then
$$\mathbb P\bigl(f(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)-\mathbb E f(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)\ge t\bigr)\le\exp\!\left(-\frac{2t^2}{V}\right),$$
and if $V=0$ this probability is $0$. The same bound holds for the lower tail, so the two-sided probability is at most $2e^{-2t^2/V}$ when $V>0$.

derivations.claim: Fix an index $k$ and let $S'$ be any sample that differs from $S$ only at coordinate $k$. Their retained samples $S\setminus k$ and $S'\setminus k$ coincide. By [F4], $|R_P(A_S)-R_P(A_{S'})|\le|R_P(A_S)-R_P(A_{S\setminus k})|+|R_P(A_{S'\setminus k})-R_P(A_{S'})|\le2\beta_m$. For every $j\ne k$, the two loss terms at the common test point $Z_j$ differ by at most $2\beta_m$, by [F2] through the same deleted output. The two $k$th loss terms each lie in $[0,M]$, so their difference is at most $M$. Hence $|\widehat R_S(A_S)-\widehat R_{S'}(A_{S'})|\le 2(m-1)\beta_m/m+M/m\le2\beta_m+M/m$. For $\Phi(S)=R_P(A_S)-\widehat R_S(A_S)$ this yields the coordinate oscillation $|\Phi(S)-\Phi(S')|\le4\beta_m+M/m$.

Fix an index $k$ and samples $S,S'$ differing only at coordinate $k$. The risk term in $\Psi(S)=R_P(A_S)-R_{\mathrm{loo}}(A,S)$ changes by at most $2\beta_m$ by [F4]. In the leave-one-out average, the $k$th term uses the same deleted training sample for $S$ and $S'$, and its test losses differ by at most $M$. For $j\ne k$, the two deleted training samples $S\setminus j$ and $S'\setminus j$ have the same $m-2$ common observations and the two alternative $k$th observations. Form a size-$m$ indexed sample $T$ from those $m-2$ common observations and both alternatives. Up to permutation, each of the two deleted training samples is obtained by deleting one of the alternatives from $T$. Permutation invariance and [F2] therefore bound their loss change at the common test point $Z_j$ by $2\beta_m$. When $m=1$ there are no indices $j\ne k$, so only the $k$th term occurs. Thus the leave-one-out average changes by at most $2(m-1)\beta_m/m+M/m\le2\beta_m+M/m$, and $|\Psi(S)-\Psi(S')|\le4\beta_m+M/m$.

Put $c=4\beta_m+M/m$. If $c=0$, then $M=\beta_m=0$ and every loss and both gaps vanish. If $c>0$, then $\Phi$ is bounded, measurable, and integrable by [A2]. Since $0<\delta<1$, [F5]–[F6] give $\log(1/\delta)>0$, so $t=c\sqrt{m\log(1/\delta)/2}>0$. The product law $P^m$ makes the coordinates independent by [F3], and [F7] with all $m$ coordinate bounds equal to $c$ gives $\mathbb P\{\Phi-\mathbb E\Phi\ge t\}\le\exp(-2t^2/(mc^2))=\delta$. By [F4], outside this event $\Phi\le2\beta_m+t=2\beta_m+(4m\beta_m+M)\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/(2m)}$. Together with the $c=0$ case this proves the first probability bound.

With $c=4\beta_m+M/m$, the case $c=0$ again has zero losses and zero gaps. If $c>0$, [A2] makes $\Psi$ bounded, measurable, and integrable. Since $0<\delta<1$, [F5]–[F6] give $\log(1/\delta)>0$. The product law $P^m$ makes the coordinates independent by [F3], and [F7] with coordinate bounds $c$ gives $\mathbb P\{\Psi-\mathbb E\Psi\ge c\sqrt{m\log(1/\delta)/2}\}\le\delta$. By [F4], $\mathbb E\Psi\le\beta_m$, so outside this event $\Psi\le\beta_m+(4m\beta_m+M)\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/(2m)}$. This proves the second probability bound, separately from the first.
